lessons.title: Who are our customers?
lessons.html:
Who are our customers?

A customer is any person or organisation that receives goods or services from the business. In a seed business it is easy to think only of the farmer who plants the seed, but there are many more customers, and each one has different needs.

External customers

Customer groupExampleMain needs
Large commercial farmersA 2 000 ha grain farmer in MpumalangaHigh yield, technical support, credit terms, timely delivery
Smallholder and emerging farmersA 5 ha maize and bean grower in KwaZulu-NatalSmall packs, affordable price, simple advice, nearby outlet
Co-operatives and agri-retailersA co-op branch selling to local farmersStock availability, margins, promotional support
Seed dealers and agentsA rural trading storeReliable supply, product training
Government and NGO programmesInput support schemes for new farmersTender compliance, large volumes, correct paperwork
Export buyersBuyers in neighbouring SADC countriesPhytosanitary documents, varieties suited to their conditions
Home gardenersVegetable seed packets at a nurseryEasy instructions, attractive packaging

Internal customers

Inside the business, departments are customers of each other. The processing plant is a customer of the seed production team, which must deliver clean seed on time. The sales team is a customer of the warehouse, which must have stock ready. When internal customers are served well, external customers benefit.

Why identify customers?

  • To offer the right products and pack sizes.
  • To give the right service and advice.
  • To plan production and stock.
  • To plan marketing activities such as farmer days and trial visits.

lessons.title: Understanding and recording customer needs
lessons.html:
Understanding and recording customer needs

Knowing who the customers are is the first step. The next step is to understand what each group needs and to keep accurate information about them.

Segmenting customers

Segmenting means dividing customers into groups with similar needs. A seed business might segment by:

  • Size: hectares planted or annual seed spend.
  • Region and climate: high-rainfall areas versus dry western areas.
  • Farming system: dryland, irrigation, conservation agriculture.
  • Crop: maize, soybeans, wheat, pasture, vegetables.
  • Channel: buys direct, through a co-op or through a dealer.

Each segment may need a different approach. A large farmer may expect a personal visit and a detailed trial report. Smallholders may be reached best through farmer days, extension officers and local radio in their language.

Sources of customer information

  • Sales records and invoices
  • Visits, phone calls and farmer days
  • Feedback and complaint records
  • Co-op and dealer reports
  • Industry information such as crop estimates and planting intentions

Keeping customer records

Record the customer's name, contact details, location, farm size, crops, products bought, preferences and any complaints. Many businesses use a customer database or CRM system. Keep information up to date and accurate.

Personal information must be protected. The Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) requires businesses to collect only what they need, keep it secure and use it only for proper purposes. Never share customer lists with outsiders.

Using the information

Review records to find customers who stopped buying, segments that are growing and products that are popular in an area. Share findings with managers to plan stock and marketing.

Key points

  • Customers include farmers, co-ops, dealers, government programmes, exporters and home gardeners.
  • Internal customers are other departments in the business.
  • Segment customers to understand different needs.
  • Keep accurate, up-to-date customer records.
  • Protect customers' personal information in line with POPIA.
